strengths: Strong empirical motivation: Section 2 provides clear, well-visualized evidence for diverse attention patterns (global/positional/semantic-dependent) and demonstrates that low-entropy tokens suffer disproportionately from KV eviction, directly motivating the reward design used later.

The two-stage training pipeline (supervised distillation from a 'Golden Eviction' oracle followed by GRPO-based RL formulated as an MDP) is a sensible and reasonably novel way to address the dynamic, non-stationary nature of KV importance that prior rule-based or one-shot trained methods miss.

Extensive experimental validation across multiple model families (Qwen3-4B/1.7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, MiniCPM-4.1-8B) and benchmarks (AIME2024/2025, GPQA, LiveCodeBench), with comparisons against a wide range of baselines (H2O, SnapKV, R-KV, RPC, G-KV, DuoAttention), consistently showing favorable results at reduced budgets.
Useful ablations isolating the contributions of the reward design, input features, and sampling strategy, which support several of the design choices rather than treating them as arbitrary.
Efficiency analysis (throughput, concurrent batch size, end-to-end speed, and overhead of the scoring model itself) substantiates the practical value of the method beyond accuracy numbers alone.

An accompanying theoretical bound (Appendix A) attempts to formally justify why minimizing evicted attention mass reduces approximation error, adding some rigor to the intuition behind Golden Eviction.
weaknesses: The theoretical result in Appendix A only bounds single-step approximation error as a function of instantaneous evicted attention mass; it does not justify the multi-step 'max over future blocks' criterion that Golden Eviction actually uses, creating a gap between the stated theoretical motivation and the proposed algorithm's long-term/future-looking design.

The overhead of generating Golden Eviction supervision (full T×T attention matrices per training sequence) and of training/storing separate scoring models per layer and attention-head group is not clearly quantified, raising reproducibility and scalability concerns, especially since a new scoring model apparently must be trained per base LLM.

Memory/latency overhead of the additional attention-feature vectors and KV concatenation used as scoring-model input is not clearly accounted for against the claimed memory savings; the paper reports scoring-model runtime overhead but not its footprint relative to the compressed cache itself.

Generalization claims are tested only on other reasoning-style benchmarks (GPQA, LiveCodeBench) despite the entropy-based motivation in Section 2.2 explicitly using summarization data; broader domain transfer (e.g., long-document QA, summarization) is not evaluated even though it was used to motivate the method.

AIME2024/2025 contain only ~30 problems each; despite 32 repeated runs, no variance/confidence intervals are reported in the main results (Figure 3), making it hard to assess the statistical significance of reported gains, particularly at the smallest budgets where curves are close together.

Baseline hyperparameters (e.g., R-KV's fixed 0.1/0.9 weighting) are taken directly from prior work without apparent re-tuning for the reasoning-model long-generation setting used here, raising some concern about comparison fairness.

The Impact Statement is boilerplate and the paper lacks an explicit, dedicated limitations discussion (e.g., training cost, per-model retraining requirement, oracle-vs-online distribution shift), which would strengthen transparency given the added system complexity introduced by the trained scoring models.

strengths: The empirical motivation in Section 2 (categorizing global/positional/semantic-dependent attention patterns, and the finding that low-entropy tokens suffer disproportionately large loss increases under eviction) is a useful and concrete observation that motivates the design choices.

The two-stage training pipeline (supervised distillation from a hindsight 'Golden Eviction' oracle followed by GRPO-based refinement under an MDP formulation) is a reasonably novel combination not previously explored for KV cache eviction, and the entropy-aware reward targeting low-entropy, high-loss-increase tokens is a sensible design choice directly tied to the Section 2.2 observations.

The experimental evaluation spans three reasoning models (Qwen3-1.7B/4B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) and two benchmarks (AIME2024/2025), with additional appendix experiments on MiniCPM-4.1-8B, GPQA, LiveCodeBench, and comparisons with more recent baselines (G-KV, DuoAttention, RPC), suggesting reasonably broad validation.

Efficiency numbers (throughput, batch size, wall-clock end-to-end speedup, and overhead of the scoring/eviction step relative to total generation time) are reported and show meaningful practical gains.
Ablations on reward design, scoring model inputs, and sampling strategy are included and help justify several design decisions.
weaknesses: The core supervision signal (Golden Eviction) relies on full-sequence future attention scores that are only available in hindsight; Table 2's comparison against R-KV/SnapKV/H2O under this oracle framing is not a fair or deployable eviction algorithm, it is merely a justification for the label-construction heuristic. The paper does not adequately discuss this oracle/hindsight mismatch with real-time deployment constraints (the RL stage is meant to address this, but how well it closes the gap versus just overfitting to the oracle-derived initialization is not rigorously isolated).

The method requires training per-model (and seemingly per-layer/per-head-group) lightweight scoring networks, plus generating oracle attention-based labels from full-length reasoning traces and running GRPO with reward computed via comparing full-model vs evicted-model losses — this training pipeline's total cost (wall-clock, GPU-hours, data requirements) is never reported or compared against the training-free baselines or against other trainable eviction baselines (e.g., Locret, AttnGate) that are discussed in Related Work but omitted from the main empirical comparisons.

Appendix A's theoretical bound (eviction error bounded by evicted attention mass) is a fairly generic/well-known result for low-rank/sparse attention approximation and does not meaningfully justify the specific design of Golden Eviction's block-wise, future-max aggregation scheme, nor does it account for compounding/recursive errors across multiple eviction steps and layers during autoregressive decoding.

Main results (Figure 3) report pass@1 averaged over 32 runs but no variance/confidence intervals are shown, making it hard to assess whether the margins over baselines (e.g., R-KV, SnapKV) are statistically meaningful, particularly at small budgets where scores fluctuate substantially across models.

The generalization claims (Section 4.3) are based on a single additional domain pair (GPQA, LiveCodeBench) using models/scorers trained only on math (STILL) data; this is a fairly narrow generalization test given how central generalization claims are to the paper's value proposition, especially since cache-eviction importance patterns could differ substantially across domains and the gains over baselines shrink noticeably at larger budgets (e.g., Table 6, 4K GPQA: 53.7 vs 50.7 for R-KV).

Limited comparison breadth in the main text: only R-KV, SnapKV, H2O are compared in the core results (Figure 3), while more relevant trainable baselines are relegated to an appendix table with fewer budget settings and not consistently replicated across all three main models/benchmarks.

The impact statement is a boilerplate single sentence, giving no real engagement with potential risks (e.g., degraded reliability in safety-critical reasoning when aggressive eviction causes factual drift, as the paper itself documents in Appendix D).

Minor presentation issues: inconsistent capitalization/notation (e.g., 'ForesightKV w.o. rl' vs 'w.o. RL' in figures), 'immediate size' likely should be 'intermediate size', and the density of symbols in Sections 3.2–3.3 makes the exposition hard to follow without closely cross-referencing the appendix.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical analysis (Section 2) identifying three distinct attention patterns (global, position-dependent, semantic-dependent) and the disproportionate loss increase on low-entropy tokens after eviction, which directly motivates the method design.

Novel two-stage training paradigm (supervised Golden Eviction + GRPO-based RL) that is, to my knowledge, the first to combine future-aware supervised labels with policy optimization for dynamic KV cache eviction, addressing a real gap between training-free heuristics and one-shot trainable methods.

The Golden Eviction algorithm is theoretically motivated (Appendix A bound on approximation error from evicted attention mass) and empirically validated (Table 2) against R-KV, SnapKV, and H2O with consistently lower loss ratios.

Extensive experimentation: three reasoning models (Qwen3-1.7B/4B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B), two primary benchmarks (AIME24/25), additional model (MiniCPM-4.1-8B), and comparisons against a wider set of recent baselines (RPC, G-KV, DuoAttention) in the appendix, lending good external validity to the claims.

Thoughtful ablations on reward design (Table 4) that empirically justify the choice of an MSE-based reward restricted to low-entropy, high-loss-increase tokens, and ablations on scoring-model inputs/sampling strategy (Table 5).
Efficiency results (Table 3, Appendix E.6) convincingly show that the scoring-model overhead is small relative to end-to-end throughput gains, supporting the practical relevance of the method.

Generalization experiments to GPQA and LiveCodeBench, despite training only on math data, strengthen the claim that the scoring model learns general eviction principles rather than overfitting to the training distribution.
weaknesses: The Golden Eviction supervision and the RL reward computation both require full (uncompressed) forward passes/attention matrices as oracles, meaning the training pipeline itself is costly; the paper does not report wall-clock/computational cost of generating training traces or training the scoring models, which is important for assessing practical reproducibility and total cost-benefit versus simpler training-free methods.

The theoretical bound in Appendix A (Proposition A.1) is a single-step, single-layer approximation-error argument; it does not rigorously justify the Golden Eviction's core multi-step future-score maximization (Eq. 5) across layers, so the "proof" partially overstates its coverage of the actual algorithm's long-term/multi-layer eviction criterion.

Training-based baseline comparisons are somewhat limited in the main text: Lancucki et al. (2025), explicitly discussed in the introduction as the representative one-shot trainable prior work, is never directly benchmarked against ForesightKV in the experiments, leaving the key motivating comparison (dynamic vs. one-time trainable importance scoring) unverified empirically.

Statistical rigor is limited: although pass@1 is averaged over 32 runs, no variance/confidence intervals are reported for any comparisons, and at larger budgets (4K) gains over strong baselines such as R-KV narrow considerably, making it hard to judge significance of the improvement in that regime.

The method requires training separate scoring models per LLM (and implicitly per attention head/group), and it is unclear how well a single trained scorer transfers across different model sizes/families or context lengths beyond the specific budgets tested (B ≤ 2K during training, tested up to 8K at most), raising questions about scalability of the training-based approach to new models in practice.

Primary evaluation is restricted to math reasoning (AIME); while GPQA/LiveCodeBench are included as generalization checks, broader long-form generation domains (e.g., open-ended dialogue, summarization beyond the brief loss-ratio study in Section 2.2) are not evaluated end-to-end with pass-rate-style metrics, somewhat limiting the generality of the main performance claims.

The Impact Statement is minimal and does not meaningfully engage with foreseeable considerations (e.g., energy/compute costs of training scoring models, or reliability implications of eviction-induced factual errors noted in Appendix D for high-stakes reasoning use cases).

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem (KV cache eviction for long reasoning generation) with a well-motivated empirical study identifying distinct attention patterns (global/positional/semantic-dependent) and the disproportionate loss increase on low-entropy tokens after eviction, which directly motivates the method design.

The two-stage training paradigm (supervised distillation from a principled 'Golden Eviction' oracle followed by GRPO-based RL that accounts for distribution shift during actual eviction-influenced decoding) is a sensible and reasonably novel combination not previously explored for KV eviction.

Extensive experimentation: three reasoning models, two AIME benchmarks with 32 repeated evaluations for statistical reliability, ablations on reward design, sampling strategy, and input features, plus a very large appendix covering scalability to 14B/32B models, additional baselines (G-KV, DuoAttention, RPC), cross-domain generalization (GPQA, LiveCodeBench, LongBench), length transfer, and throughput/latency analysis.
Clear efficiency gains are demonstrated (up to ~9.79x throughput improvement at low budgets) with negligible overhead from the scoring model itself (~2.7% of total generation time).
Attempted theoretical justification (Appendix A) connecting the Golden Eviction surrogate to bounds on attention-output/loss perturbation, adding some principled grounding beyond pure heuristics.
weaknesses: The closest prior training-based baseline explicitly discussed in the introduction and related work (Lancucki et al., 2025) is never empirically compared against in any experiment, leaving the core claimed advantage over other 'one-time judgment' trainable eviction methods unverified.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix A relies on several loose/strong assumptions (bounded value norms, local Lipschitzness of the logit and loss mappings, a multiplicative factor Ht that can be large) and mainly justifies the block-level surrogate used for label construction rather than the actual learned scoring model or the RL-refined policy, so its practical guarantees are limited.

The reward design (MSE loss on low-entropy, high-loss-increase tokens with a fixed margin η=1.5 and 80% threshold) appears to require nontrivial manual tuning; while some sensitivity analysis is provided in the appendix, the choices seem empirically selected rather than principled, raising concerns about robustness to new domains or models without re-tuning.

The scoring model's input features (multiple attention window sizes, decayed cumulative sums, raw key/value concatenation) add considerable engineering complexity and hyperparameters, which may hinder reproducibility and easy adaptation to different architectures (e.g., differing GQA group sizes, hidden dimensions).

Evaluation is centered on AIME2024/2025, which are small benchmarks (30 problems each); although pass@1 is averaged over 32 runs, the primary comparisons and most ablations rely on this narrow, math-specific evaluation before appendix generalization experiments are added.

No explicit discussion of limitations or failure modes of the method (e.g., cases where the scoring model or RL training might fail, sensitivity to distillation data quality/domain, memory/compute cost of training the scoring models across all layers and heads) is provided in the main text, and the Impact Statement is essentially a boilerplate placeholder.

strengths: The empirical motivation in Section 2 (categorizing attention patterns into global/positional/semantic-dependent, and the loss-increase analysis for low-entropy vs. high-entropy tokens) is well-presented and provides a clear rationale for the proposed reward design.

Extensive experimental coverage: three main reasoning models (Qwen3-1.7B/4B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) on AIME2024/2025, plus appendix experiments extending to Qwen3-14B/32B, MiniCPM-4.1-8B, GPQA, LiveCodeBench, and LongBench, which strengthens the generality claims.

A reasonably thorough set of ablations (reward design, sampling strategy, model inputs, entropy threshold sensitivity, length transfer) that help isolate the contribution of individual design choices.
Clear efficiency gains are demonstrated (throughput/#MCB improvements and low overhead of the eviction mechanism itself), which is directly relevant to the stated motivation of the paper.

An attempt at theoretical justification (Appendix A) connecting the Golden Eviction surrogate to an upper bound on attention-output and loss perturbation, giving some principled grounding to the label-construction heuristic.
weaknesses: The method requires training lightweight scoring models per LLM (and apparently per attention group/layer), with a two-stage SFT+RL pipeline that needs generating long reasoning traces with the base model, computing Golden Eviction labels, and running GRPO; the paper reports non-trivial training costs (e.g., 8h×2 + 6h×8 GPUs for a 7B model). This undermines the practical appeal relative to training-free baselines and is not clearly justified against amortized throughput savings in a cost-benefit analysis.

The RL stage (Section 3.3) appears to sample multiple eviction traces over a fixed, previously generated sequence w rather than re-generating tokens conditioned on the evicted cache; this constitutes a teacher-forced approximation of the MDP that does not account for how eviction would actually alter the autoregressive generation trajectory at inference time. This potential train/inference mismatch is not discussed or validated.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix A relies on fairly strong simplifying assumptions (bounded value norms, local Lipschitz continuity of the output-to-logit and logit-to-loss mappings) that are not verified empirically, so the 'proof' functions more as a loose motivating sketch than a rigorous guarantee, and this should be stated more clearly as a limitation.

The reward formulation (low-entropy token subset selection via an entropy threshold and loss-increase threshold η) introduces multiple sensitive hyperparameters; sensitivity analysis is only provided for a single model/budget/benchmark combination, leaving open whether these choices generalize robustly.

Baselines in the main comparison (SnapKV, H2O, R-KV) are all training-free; more informative comparisons against other trainable KV-eviction approaches (e.g., Lancucki et al., 2025, discussed in related work but not benchmarked) are missing from the main results, which would better position the paper's claimed novelty of combining SFT and RL.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported in the main results figures despite averaging over 32 runs per benchmark, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported gains, especially given the relatively small AIME test sets.
The overall presentation is dense and notation-heavy (especially Sections 3.2–3.3 and Appendix A), which may hinder reproducibility and accessibility despite the code release.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical analysis (Section 2) identifying three attention pattern types and demonstrating that low-entropy tokens suffer disproportionately large loss increases after KV eviction, which directly motivates the method design.

The two-stage training pipeline (Golden Eviction + pairwise ranking supervised learning, followed by GRPO-based RL with an MDP formulation) is a sensible and novel combination for addressing the dynamic, future-dependent nature of KV pair importance, distinguishing it from prior one-shot or rule-based eviction methods.

Extensive experimental validation: three main reasoning models (Qwen3-1.7B/4B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) on AIME2024/2025, plus additional experiments on larger models (Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B), another architecture (MiniCPM-4.1-8B), and more baselines (RPC, G-KV, DuoAttention) in the appendix, showing consistent and often substantial improvements over SnapKV/H2O/R-KV.

Thorough ablation studies covering reward function design (Table 4), scoring model inputs and sampling strategy (Table 5), entropy threshold sensitivity, length transfer, and reward generalization across domains/models, which support the design choices rather than treating them as fixed.

Theoretical appendix (Appendix A) provides a principled, if approximate, justification connecting the Golden Eviction surrogate objective to bounded attention-output perturbation and downstream loss drift.

Strong demonstrated efficiency gains (up to ~9.79x throughput, substantial increase in max concurrent batch size) and an accounting of the eviction mechanism's own overhead (Appendix E.9), suggesting practical viability.

Generalization experiments beyond the training domain (GPQA, LiveCodeBench, LongBench) support the claim that the learned scoring model captures general notions of KV importance rather than overfitting to math reasoning.
weaknesses: The method is not training-free: it requires constructing Golden Eviction traces (which itself needs full attention computation over long sequences) and training per-model scoring models, adding nontrivial offline cost; only one training-cost example (7B model) is reported, leaving the cost-scaling behavior for other budgets/models unclear.

The scoring model's own inference-time overhead (extra MLP forward passes using concatenated K/V representations and multi-scale attention features) is only partially quantified (Appendix E.9 for one setting), and it is unclear whether this overhead is consistently negligible across all budgets, sequence lengths, and hardware setups.

The theoretical bound in Appendix A relies on fairly strong assumptions (bounded value norms, local Lipschitz continuity of the logit and loss mappings) and is primarily a qualitative justification for the one-step-ahead surrogate rather than a tight guarantee relevant to the multi-step, non-stationary eviction process actually used at inference.

No variance or confidence intervals are reported for the pass@1 scores despite averaging over 32 runs per benchmark; given the small size and inherent noise of AIME2024/2025, statistical significance of the reported gains (especially smaller margins) is not established.

The approach introduces several additional hyperparameters (eviction length L, candidate set size 2L for sampling, reward margin η, KL coefficient β per model) that appear to require per-model tuning, which could limit ease of adoption and reproducibility without the exact released configs.

The MDP/RL formulation assumes a frozen base LLM and trains lightweight scoring models per attention head/group, but the paper does not clearly discuss how the number of scoring-model parameters scales with model size (heads x layers), which could become a practical concern for very large models.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential considerations (e.g., resource/environmental costs of the two-stage training itself, or reliability risks from more aggressive cache compression in deployed reasoning systems).
